newsitem.title: USA: N.J. Senate campaign gets dirty.
newsitem.headline: N.J. Senate campaign gets dirty.

text.p: New Jersey has long been the butt of jokes about dirty air and dirty water. Now add another insult -- dirty politics.
Republican Dick Zimmer and Democrat Robert Torricelli are slinging insults and hurling mud in the heated race for the U.S. Senate seat being vacated by retiring three-term Democrat Bill Bradley.
The open seat is highly coveted, with Republicans hoping to strengthen their 53-47 majority in the Senate and Democrats aiming to keep the seat on their side of the aisle.
Candidates Zimmer and Torricelli, both veterans of the House of Representatives, are accusing one another of such sins as taking mob-stained money and missing hundreds of votes in Congress.

Republican campaign commercials paint Torricelli as an "ethically challenged" tax-and-spend liberal. Democratic ads call Zimmer "ethically unfit" and willing to accept donations from corporate polluters.

Largely to blame for all the political name-calling is New Jersey's peculiar position as a state with no media centre, analysts say. Candidates must rely instead on media coverage in New York City and Philadelphia -- and New Jersey politics are not a particulary sexy story in either city.

Accordingly, two-thirds of New Jersey's four million voters polled recently never heard of either candidate. Compounding the problem, there is no high-profile statewide job such as Lieutenant Governor to give politicians a publicity boost.

"Both candidates are so much of an unknown commodity to the electorate you can say almost anything you want," said Cliff Zukin, a professor of political science at the Eagleton Institute at Rutgers University in New Brunswick, N.J.
"If people knew more about these candidates, they wouldn't be able to get away with as many outrageous claims," he said.

With no steady media coverage to count on, candidates in New Jersey rely heavily on paid advertising. Each campaign is estimated to be spending up to $8 million, making this Senate race among the most expensive in the nation.

Boosting the cost of the race is the fractured nature of New Jersey's media market. Candidates must buy time in New York City, the nation's pricey No. 1 market, and Philadelphia, the fourth-largest market. Yet those ads are wasted on two-thirds of viewers in each market who don't live or vote in New Jersey.

Having just minutes of television time to send a message, candidates must hit as hard as they can, analysts said. "It's much easier to paint a negative image of someone else than to paint a positive image of yourself," Zukin said.
Although each campaign is tainting the other as extremist, under all the mud are two pro-choice moderates, analysts note.

"They're both well-educated, intelligent, hard-working, experienced people with fairly distinct policy perspectives, and that's what's really not coming out in this campaign," said David Rebovich, a political scientist at Rider College in Lawrenceville, N.J., who calls this "the dirtiest campaign in the country."

Torricelli, 45, an outspoken lawyer, has served three terms in Congress. He captured national attention for accusing the Central Intelligence Agency of supporting violence in Guatemala and for dating Bianca Jagger, the ex-wife of rock star Mick Jagger.

Zimmer, 52, is considered a fiscal conservative and social moderate like the state's popular Gov. Christine Whitman. In Congress for six years, he is known for sponsoring "Megan's Law," which requires communities be notified when a convicted sex offender moves in.

Recent polls show a statistical dead heat -- Torricelli with 39 percent, Zimmer with 33 percent and 20 percent undecided. Pivotal to the outcome are the independents, who weigh in at a hefty 53 percent of the state's voters.
Polls also show negative campaigning could keep voters away from the polls altogether.
But experts such as local political author Stephen Salmore say this race does not deserve the down-and-dirty label.

"It's fairly nasty, but as New Jersey races go, it's not particularly nasty," he said, citing previous races by Sen. Frank Lautenberg and former Gov. Jim Florio. "Negative harsh races are nothing new," he said.
Zimmer and Torricelli plan two debates, on Oct. 5 and 17.
